supplement.where: Appendix 1: AI augmented ideation tool, PDF pp. 28-29 (printed pp. xxvi-xxvii), referenced in Section 4.1 on PDF p. 13. No external supplement is identified.
supplement.holds: Four screenshots of the tool overview, persona generation, persona contributions, and task-solution input. No additional outcome statistics, SDs, SEs, or confidence intervals are supplied in this appendix.

paper_design_summary: University of Regensburg students were randomly assigned to a custom GPT-4 Turbo ideation tool or no AI, then worked in teams on elderly-healthcare and automotive business-model proposals. The paper reports 70 students in 24 teams producing 48 ideas; blinded experts scored idea quality, and Task 1 proposals were also classified by innovation type (PDF pp. 4 and 12-15). The dedicated sessions in separate rooms and at team stations are coded lab_rct under the codebook, although the authors call the study a framed/controlled field experiment (PDF pp. 1 and 13-14).

studies.label: Team ideation experiment: elderly healthcare and automotive business models

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants were randomly assigned to the experimental or control condition and then organized into teams. The experimental condition received the custom GenAI tool; control received no AI. The same condition applied to both tasks. The randomization procedure and allocation ratio are not stated.
assignment.quote: In the first phase, participants are randomly assigned to either an experimental group or a control group.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 12 (printed p. 10), Section 4, experimental phases; corroborated on PDF p. 4 (printed p. 2), Section 1, and p. 25 (printed p. 23), Section 7.

arms.name: GenAI-assisted team ideation
arms.description: Teams received an introduction and Q&A about the custom GenAI tool, then used it to develop and submit consensus solutions to both tasks. The tool generated and conversed through tailored AI expert personas (PDF pp. 13-14, Section 4.1).

arms.name: Team ideation without AI
arms.description: Teams brainstormed without AI after a brief introduction, using the same tasks and background information, and submitted through Google Forms; they worked in a separate room and were not told that the experimental condition used AI (PDF pp. 12-15, Sections 4-4.2).

participants.exclusions: The paper reports 70 students in 24 teams generating 48 ideas, but does not separately state how many people were represented in the final analysis. Neither an assignment-stage nor a final analyzed headcount is explicitly enumerated, so n_randomized and n_analyzed are null. Exclusions, withdrawals, allocation ratio, and per-arm people counts are not reported; missing attrition information does not establish zero attrition. The description of three-person teams is not reconciled with 70 students in 24 teams (PDF pp. 12-15, Sections 4-4.2). The output-level results and the included appendix supply no participant flow or final people count (PDF p. 18, Tables 2-3; pp. 28-29, Appendix 1).
participants.who: University of Regensburg business, economics, and information systems students with coursework in International Management and Strategic Management; they had limited exposure to healthcare and automotive innovation (PDF pp. 13-14, Section 4.1). The country is not expressly stated in the participant description.
participants.quote: The study involved 70 students in 24 teams, generating 48 unique ideas.
participants.locator: PDF p. 14 (printed p. 12), Section 4.1, participant, sample, and consent paragraphs; University of Regensburg identified on PDF p. 13 (printed p. 11). PDF p. 15 (printed p. 13), Sections 4.2-5, describes output-level analysis; PDF p. 18, Tables 2-3, and pp. 28-29, Appendix 1, provide no final analyzed people count.

ai_tool.name_model: Custom GenAI-assisted creativity support system based on OpenAI GPT-4 Turbo (PDF p. 4, Section 1); methods also call the backend GPT-4 (PDF p. 13, Section 4.1).
ai_tool.how_used: Teams entered a problem and conversed with four AI expert personas tailored to that problem, receiving ideas, insights, and feedback; revised problem descriptions could regenerate the personas. Automated prompts reused the conversation transcript. Teams submitted solutions through the interface once consensus was reached. The stated temperature setting was zero (PDF p. 13, Section 4.1; interface screenshots on PDF pp. 28-29, Appendix 1).

task.description: Each team produced a concrete solution proposal for each of two tasks: a product/service innovation in healthcare for seniors and an automotive business-model innovation considering autonomous driving. The two tasks used the same participant sample and conditions (PDF p. 12, Section 4).
task.duration: 45-minute maximum task duration, with earlier submission allowed (PDF p. 14, printed p. 12, Section 4.1); this preserves the source wording.

outcomes.name: Aggregated idea-quality score
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Aggregate of the expert-rated Dean et al. idea-quality dimensions; the aggregation formula and weights are not specified. This is the main overall score discussed under H1, but no outcome is explicitly designated primary. Blinded domain-expert panel rated team solution proposals using the Dean et al. framework on a 7-point Likert scale (PDF p. 12, Section 4, and p. 15, Section 4.2). The analysis compares mean quality scores per idea; the two tasks are combined (PDF p. 15, Sections 4.2-5). The reported corpus contains 48 ideas (PDF p. 14, Section 4.1); no outcome-specific omissions are stated. Figures 2-3 show distributions and arm means, Figure 4 shows p-values from 1000 bootstrap variations, and Figure 5 plots Cohen's d (PDF pp. 16-20). These are analyses of the same outcome. Numerical SDs, SEs, confidence intervals, and exact numerical Cohen's d values are not printed; Figure 3 has error bars without a stated definition. No adjustment for repeated ideas from the same team is described. Table 3 labels its coefficient column t-test, but the accompanying text identifies those entries as regression coefficients (PDF pp. 18-19).

contrasts.reported: Mean: Experimental (E) 4.583, Control (C) 3.546. Table 2: t = -4.450938, p = 0.000056. Table 3: coefficient (column headed t-test) = 1.037037, p = 0.000054, R-squared = 0.301027. No numerical SD, SE, or confidence interval is reported. Cohen's d is plotted without numerical bar labels in Figure 5. The accompanying prose states Cohen's d above 0.8 for this outcome (PDF p. 20).
contrasts.locator: PDF pp. 16-17 (printed pp. 14-15), Section 5, means paragraph and Figure 3; PDF p. 18 (printed p. 16), Tables 2-3, Aggregated row; PDF pp. 19-20 (printed pp. 17-18), Figures 4-5 and accompanying text.

outcomes.name: Revolutionary innovation classification
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Indicator that an idea was classified as revolutionary under the Abernathy and Clark innovation matrix. The panel classified ideas by their impact on existing technological competencies and market relationships (PDF p. 8, Section 2.2; p. 12, Section 4; p. 15, Section 4.2). Only Task 1 ideas were included in the innovation-type analysis because the predefined autonomous-driving problem in Task 2 could bias classification (PDF p. 17, Section 5; p. 20, Section 5). A point-biserial correlation relates AI assistance to each category. The four categories are recorded as separate reported indicators of one nominal classification; they are not a measure of diversity across teams or an ordered creativity scale. No category counts or percentages, or explicit number of ideas analyzed for this task-specific test, are printed.

company_involvement.description: No company affiliation, funding, sponsorship, or company role in conducting the study is disclosed. eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is met: participants were explicitly randomly assigned to GenAI assistance or no AI while producing their team proposals (PDF p. 12, Section 4; pp. 13-14, Section 4.1). Criterion 2 is unclear under the current form spec, which counts people analyzed: the paper reports 70 students in 24 teams generating 48 ideas, but does not explicitly identify the final analyzed people count or provide exclusions, withdrawals, or participant flow (PDF p. 14, Section 4.1). The reported study sample cannot be treated as a confirmed final analyzed headcount; n_analyzed is null. The descriptions of three-person teams and 70 students in 24 teams are also unreconciled (PDF pp. 12 and 14). Neither the output-level results nor the included appendix settles the count (PDF pp. 15-20, Sections 4.2-5; pp. 28-29, Appendix 1). This does not establish that fewer than 50 people were analyzed. Criterion 3 is met: blinded experts scored the submitted proposals, including originality and aggregate idea quality, using a 7-point scale (PDF pp. 4, 12, and 15; results on pp. 16-18). Dedicated sessions in separate rooms and at team stations support lab_rct under the codebook (PDF pp. 13-14). Missing precision accounting for repeated team outputs affects pooling rather than these screening criteria. Core eligibility remains unclear pending confirmation of at least 50 distinct people in the final analysis.

one_line_finding: AI-assisted teams received higher aggregate idea-quality ratings (4.583 vs 3.546; t = -4.450938, p = 0.000056; PDF pp. 16-18, Figure 3 and Table 2).
open_questions: The paper reports 70 students in 24 teams generating 48 ideas but does not explicitly give the final analyzed people count; criterion 2 remains unclear. Actual team sizes, per-arm people counts, the assignment-stage headcount, and any post-assignment exclusions or withdrawals are also undocumented, and the three-person-team description is not reconciled with the stated sample (PDF pp. 12-15).

The main analysis combines ideas from both tasks without reporting team-clustered precision or a mixed model. The bootstrap resampling unit is unstated; independent-unit precision is needed before pooling (PDF pp. 15 and 18-20).
Numerical SDs, SEs, confidence intervals, exact Cohen's d values, the d standardizer, the aggregate-score formula/weights, and the meaning of Figure 3 error bars are not supplied (PDF pp. 15-20).

The source calls the experiment a field experiment, while the described dedicated sessions support lab_rct under this codebook. Additional documentation would be needed to establish ordinary-coursework delivery (PDF pp. 12-14).

The prose calls paradigm-relatedness and acceptability medium effects, but their Figure 5 bars exceed its large-effect reference line. Preserve this source discrepancy without estimating exact d values (PDF p. 20).

There are five substantive A-versus-B differences: the one-versus-four innovation-category representation and four outcome-specific additions of a narrative Cohen's d > 0.8 threshold. Outcome aliases, arm labels, locators that identify the same source passage, equivalent task-duration wording, and a blank versus an explicit not-stated sample-overlap field are not counted as substantive differences. All design and assignment codes, arm AI status, people counts, task type, AI model/role, the first ten outcomes' construct/question/measure/unit/availability/timing/primary fields, every tabulated number and test direction, supplement status, company-disclosure status, eligibility criteria, and main finding agree substantively. A shared author-name transcription error was corrected from the cover and documented among agreed-field checks; it does not inflate n_differences. The five differences are resolved; n_unresolved counts unresolved differences, not the separate source-reporting limitations listed in open_questions.

One experiment is coded. The two ideation tasks share teams; the second project phase is expert evaluation, not another experiment. The fifteen tool-development participants across three usability studies have no separately reported comparative creativity outcomes and are not added to the main sample (PDF p. 13). The 70-person count is retained only as the reported study sample. The paper does not explicitly identify the people represented in the final analysis; n_analyzed is null, and no assignment-stage or per-arm headcount or absence of attrition is inferred. Country is not expressly supplied in the participant description. Dedicated rooms, stations, and timed tasks support lab_rct under the codebook, despite the authors' controlled/framed field-experiment terminology; ordinary-coursework delivery is unconfirmed.

All fourteen outcomes are retained: aggregate quality, nine component ratings, and four category-specific indicators of the same nominal innovation classification. The category indicators are mutually dependent, use only Task 1, have no explicit Task 1 analysis count, and are not distinct studies or measures of diversity across people. No paper-designated or preregistered primary outcome is stated; aggregate quality is listed first by the codebook preference. Quality t-tests, regressions, bootstrap checks, and Cohen's d plots are alternative analyses of the same outcomes. The paper reports no participant- or team-adjusted precision, and the bootstrap resampling unit is unstated.

H4's diversity claim is operationalized through originality, paradigm relevance, and feasibility ratings of individual outputs, without an across-team similarity or dispersion statistic (PDF p. 11, Table 1; pp. 14-21). There is no across_people or after_ai outcome. Time, quality/time efficiency, and self-reported satisfaction/engagement are not output-scored creativity/diversity outcomes (PDF pp. 11, 17, and 21). The statement about increased idea output per unit time does not report a separate fluency comparison.

Means, t statistics, p-values, coefficients, and R-squared are preserved as printed; no effect size or standard error was computed. Figure 3 error bars have no stated definition. The broad claim that all dimensions differ significantly is contradicted for applicability by Tables 2-3 and the conclusion (PDF pp. 16-18 and 26); applicability is coded no_clear_difference. The Figure 5/text discrepancy for paradigm-relatedness and acceptability is preserved in open_questions. Retained 70 solely as the reported study sample. Changed eligibility.criterion_2_at_least_50_people and eligibility.core to unclear. The source supplies no participant flow or explicit analysis-stage headcount; missing attrition reporting cannot verify that all 70 were analyzed. Assignment-stage and per-arm counts remain null. The unchanged historical reconciliation is superseded on this point by the final decision.

open_items.item: Final analyzed people count (open_questions[0], criterion 2): author confirmation is needed of the distinct students represented in the analyzed proposals and whether that total is at least 50. Participant flow, actual team sizes, and allocation by arm would also explain the reported 70 students in 24 teams versus the three-person-team description; those ancillary counts must not be inferred (PDF pp. 12-15).

Independent-unit precision and bootstrap resampling unit (open_questions[1]): data and analysis code linking both task outputs to teams, together with resampling definitions, would establish or permit precision accounting for repeated team outputs. This affects pooling, not any of the three screening criteria (PDF pp. 15 and 18-20). No suitable posted files were verified in this review.

Missing numerical SDs, SEs, confidence intervals, exact Cohen's d values and standardizer, aggregate-score formula/weights, and Figure 3 error-bar definition (open_questions[2]): author documentation or the original analysis output would settle these extraction questions. They do not undermine the confirmed expert scoring of outputs or otherwise decide eligibility; the included appendix supplies none of these details (PDF pp. 15-20 and 28-29).

Lab versus field setting (open_questions[3]): dedicated sessions support the retained lab_rct code; author documentation of ordinary-coursework delivery would settle the remaining context question raised by the paper's field-experiment label. Both randomized setting classes satisfy criterion 1, so this distinction does not affect eligibility (PDF pp. 12-14).

Figure 5 versus prose effect-size descriptions (open_questions[4]): the prose calls paradigm-relatedness and acceptability medium effects, while their bars exceed the figure's large-effect reference line. Author confirmation of the intended Cohen's d values or a corrected figure/text would settle the discrepancy. It concerns effect magnitude, not eligibility; no bar heights are converted to numerical effects (PDF p. 20).
